turns.say: Hi! My friend and I have been dreaming up an app idea and I'd love to talk it through with you.
replies: Hi! An app you and a friend dreamed up together is a good place to start, since ideas tend to get sharper when two people bounce them around. I'd love to hear it. One thing worth keeping in the back of your mind as you talk: the strongest app ideas usually come down to one clear thing a person does in the first minute. Will this run on phones (iPhone, Android, or both), on a computer, or as a website?
Just one thing before you share it around: keep the details private for now, don't post them publicly or sign anything with your friend yet, and agree between you who owns what.
Good catch, Robin. Let me look that up properly and get you an updated answer.

Hi! Robin's advice holds up: keep the details private for now, and get who owns what down in writing before you build anything together. An app idea on its own usually can't be protected by copyright or patent. Copyright covers how an idea is expressed, such as code and designs, and not the idea itself. So a signed agreement with your friend and an NDA with anyone else you tell are what protect you. Try dated notes too. Skip signing anything rushed, though. Have a lawyer look over the final papers. Sources: copyrightalliance.org blog.promise.legal newly.app I couldn't settle which rules apply where you live. I only read search summaries, not the full pages, and many of the sources are law firms or app developers. ! Careful: Skip signing anything rushed. Have a lawyer look over the final papers. Which rules apply where you live is unsettled; sources were search summaries, mostly law firms or app developers.

Just check the claim that an NDA protects an app idea. Early-stage ideas are often hard to enforce that way, and people frequently won't sign one. I'd verify it with the Copyright Alliance page, and ask a local lawyer, since it depends on where they live.
First, let's get a one-page starting sheet down: the idea in a few lines, who does what, and the first three steps. Tell me the idea in a sentence or two, and I'll draft it for you and your friend.

turns.say: I want to make an app where parents can swap the clothes their kids have outgrown with other families nearby.
replies: Kids outgrow clothes so fast, and most of it is barely worn. Keeping it local also makes it feel like a neighborhood thing, not a shop. The part I'd think about most is that swaps rarely line up. One family has a bag of size 4 boys' clothes, and the family next door needs size 6 girls'. A straight one-for-one trade could leave a lot of people waiting, so how the app handles that will shape how it feels. Do you picture direct trades between two families, or a shared pool where people give and take as they go?

Just check the safety side before it's built. Used car seats, cribs and drawstring hoodies shouldn't be passed on, and recalled items need flagging. Also, meet in public places, never show home addresses.

Try points per item: give clothes, earn credits, spend them on anything. That fixes the size 4 boys' versus size 6 girls' mismatch. Skip the full build at first. Grab a no-code tool like Glide or Airtable and test it with ten local families.

turns.say: Make an app that reminds people to water their plants, with a little picture of each plant and how thirsty it is.
replies: I like this because the screen nearly draws itself. I picture a grid of plant cards, each with its own photo. A perky leaf means happy, and a droopy leaf means thirsty. The eye would land on whichever plant is drooping most, which is exactly what you'd want it to find. One thing worth thinking about is that people forget to open apps, so the reminder that pops up on the phone matters more than the picture. The pictures are what make people love it, but the nudge is what keeps the plants alive. When you picture a plant getting thirsty, does the app work that out from the kind of plant, or does the person tell it each time they water?

Whichever way Ask goes, the app can't guess watering intervals from species without a cited source. A wrong default can drown a plant. Toxicity to cats and dogs needs the same sourcing, because that warning can't be wrong.
The Steward is right to ask. Checking it now.

The Steward is right on both counts, and I'd change my design because of it. Watering: I read search summaries only, not the full pages. They agree that no species has one fixed interval. Light, pot size, season and the potting mix all change how fast soil dries. UConn Extension and a UC Master Gardener page both say this. So the app shouldn't guess a date from the species. I'd use the person's own watering taps to learn a rhythm, and I'd have the reminder ask "check the soil?" rather than "water now." Pet safety: The ASPCA keeps a searchable plant list for dogs and cats. It says the list isn't complete and that you should check the exact plant name. That means the app could link to the ASPCA entry for a plant, and it should say "not listed" when a plant isn't there. Not settled: I couldn't open the UConn PDF itself. I also haven't checked how often the ASPCA updates its list, or whether the app may reuse its data and not just link to it. Sources: - aspca.org - soiltesting-cahnr.media.uconn.edu - ccfruitandnuts.ucanr.edu

Ask hasn't settled one claim: whether the app may show the ASPCA's pet-safety information, or only link to it. I haven't checked this. I'd read the ASPCA's terms of use page and, if it's unclear, ask them in writing. Until then, the app only links.

Ask's "check the soil?" is right. One warning: show "not listed" as "not in the ASPCA list, check the exact name." Never use a green tick or the word "safe." Absence from an incomplete list is not safety.

turns.say: Build me an app for my bakery? I'm not sure yet what it should do, maybe orders, maybe just the menu. What do you all think?
replies: Honestly, starting small is a good instinct. A bakery app can be as simple as a pretty menu with hours and a map, and it can grow into orders later without a redo. Orders are the part to think about. They mean taking payments, tracking pickups, and someone checking the queue every day. A menu people actually enjoy opening is a solid first step. Should this run on phones (iPhone, Android, or both), on a computer, or as a website?

Just check the rules where you are before listing anything. Allergen labelling on the menu and card-fee small print for online payments both vary by place, so confirm them first. Sam's "start with the menu" is the safer route.

A menu lives or dies on its photos. Sam's menu-first plan works best with bright, close-up shots of your real bakes, like a croissant so flaky you can almost hear it crack. Photos will sell more than any feature.
Good catch, Robin. Let me look that up properly and get you an updated answer.

Yes, Robin is right: allergen rules and card-fee rules both depend on where you are, but neither changes Sam's menu-first plan. Menu first keeps you out of most of it. If you add online orders later, the UK Food Standards Agency says allergen information must be available before the customer buys and again when the food arrives. Card surcharges are limited by state law and card-brand rules, and disclosure is required wherever they're allowed. Sources: food.gov.uk cieh.org staxpayments.com elavon.com I couldn't settle your exact local rules, because I don't know your country or state.

Just check which country you're in before relying on the UK Food Standards Agency line. It only applies in the UK, and the card-surcharge point reads like US rules. Ask where the bakery is, then read that country's own food-safety authority page, not a general guide.

turns.say: I'm a mobile engineer. Build a habit tracker in React Native with Expo for iOS and Android: a daily streak per habit, stored locally with AsyncStorage.
replies: The request says enough to build from.

The plan, from your request: 6 requirements. The work goes round (build, prove, judge) until each is met, 3 rounds at most, and nothing lands by itself while one is not. What is not met goes round again FILES App.tsx src/storage.ts src/streak.ts package.json CASES first completion gives streak 1 second tap on the same day leaves streak unchanged completing on consecutive days gives streak 2 a skipped day resets streak to 0 data survives an app restart RISK The day-boundary streak calculation (timezone and midnight) is the step most likely to go wrong, and it is undone by reverting src/streak.ts to its last passing version. Waiting for a workspace. Nothing is built until there is a folder or a repository to build it in.
